```{=html}
<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Appendix B <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Proofs &amp; Comments</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">B.22</span> Torsion in Newton-Cartan Theory (§<a class="dg-xref" href="../newtonian/newtonian-spacetime.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Newtonian_Spacetime">9.1</a>)</h1></header>
<p>Two statements about torsion are frequently encountered, and seem to contradict each other: “torsion does not affect the autoparallels, since the autoparallel equation only involves the symmetric part of the connection coefficient functions”, and “torsion does affect the autoparallels”. Both are correct. They differ in <em>what is held fixed</em> when torsion is introduced: either the symmetric part of the connection coefficient functions, or some other structure from which the connection is constructed, such as a metric. Torsion is written as in Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Covariant_Derivative">6</a>, <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}^i_{jk} = \Gamma^i_{kj} - \Gamma^i_{jk}\)</span>, with <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^i_{jk} = dx^i\left\lceil \nabla_{\partial x_k} \partial x_j \right\rfloor\)</span>. Even when torsion leaves the autoparallels unchanged, it does affect parallel transport and curvature, which is why the torsion-free condition in the definition of Newtonian spacetime matters (Subsections <a class="dg-xref" href="#subsection_Torsion_Parallel_Transport" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_Torsion_Parallel_Transport">B.22.4</a> and <a class="dg-xref" href="#subsection_Torsion_Newtonian" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_Torsion_Newtonian">B.22.5</a>).</p>
```

## `<span class="dg-secnum">B.22.1</span> Statement A: the Symmetric Part is Held Fixed`{=html} {#subsection_Torsion_Statement_A}

```{=html}
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>Every connection coefficient function splits into its symmetric and antisymmetric parts in the two lower indices,  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \Gamma^i_{jk} = \Gamma^i_{(jk)} + \Gamma^i_{[jk]},
            \qquad
            \Gamma^i_{[jk]} \coloneqq \frac{1}{2} \Big[ \Gamma^i_{jk} - \Gamma^i_{kj} \Big] = - \frac{1}{2} \, \mathtt{T}^i_{jk},
        \end{align*}</span>  so the antisymmetric part <em>is</em> the torsion, up to a factor <span class="math inline">\(-1/2\)</span>, while the symmetric part is independent of it. Since in the autoparallel equation  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \ddot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U} + \Gamma^k_{ji} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}
            = \ddot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U} + \Gamma^k_{(ji)} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U} = 0
        \end{align*}</span>  the coefficient functions are contracted with the symmetric product <span class="math inline">\(\dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}\)</span>, the antisymmetric part drops out.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Statement A.</strong> Two connections with the same symmetric part, <span class="math inline">\(\tilde{\Gamma}^k_{(ij)} = \Gamma^k_{(ij)}\)</span>, have the same autoparallels, whatever their torsions. Without charts: the difference of two connections is a <span class="math inline">\((1,2)\)</span>-tensor field <span class="math inline">\(S\)</span> (Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Covariant_Derivative">6</a>), and both connections have the same autoparallels if and only if <span class="math inline">\(S\)</span> is antisymmetric in its two vector slots, i.e. if they differ only by torsion.</p></li>
<li><p>This is the right statement whenever the connection itself is the primary structure, freely specified by its coefficient functions, as in the Newtonian spacetime of Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../newtonian/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Newtonian">9</a>.</p></li>
</ul>
```

## `<span class="dg-secnum">B.22.2</span> Statement B: a Metric is Held Fixed`{=html} {#subsection_Torsion_Statement_B}

```{=html}
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>In most physical theories the connection is not specified freely but <em>constructed</em> from other structures, subject to compatibility conditions. The standard case is a <strong>metric</strong>: a symmetric <span class="math inline">\((0,2)\)</span>-tensor field <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span> whose matrix of component functions <span class="math inline">\(g_{ij} \coloneqq g(\partial x_i, \partial x_j)\)</span> is invertible at every point, with inverse <span class="math inline">\(g^{ij}\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(g^{ik} g_{kj} = \delta^i_j\)</span>. A connection is <strong>metric compatible</strong> if <span class="math inline">\(\nabla g = 0\)</span>, i.e. if parallel transport preserves the lengths of and angles between vectors. Writing <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma_{kij} \coloneqq g_{km} \Gamma^m_{ij}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}_{kij} \coloneqq g_{km} \mathtt{T}^m_{ij}\)</span>, the condition reads  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            0 = \big( \nabla_{\partial x_k} g \big)(\partial x_i, \partial x_j)
            = \partial x_k\left\lfloor g_{ij} \right\rceil - \Gamma_{jik} - \Gamma_{ijk}.
        \end{align*}</span></p></li>
<li><p>Given <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span> and a prescribed torsion <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}\)</span>, there is exactly <em>one</em> metric compatible connection with that torsion<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-10" id="fnref-10" role="doc-noteref" aria-label="Footnote 10">10</a></sup>:  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \Gamma_{kij} =
            \underbrace{\frac{1}{2} \Big[ \partial x_i\left\lfloor g_{jk} \right\rceil + \partial x_j\left\lfloor g_{ki} \right\rceil - \partial x_k\left\lfloor g_{ij} \right\rceil \Big]}_{\eqqcolon \, \mathring{\Gamma}_{kij}}
            + \underbrace{\frac{1}{2} \Big[ \mathtt{T}_{kji} + \mathtt{T}_{jki} + \mathtt{T}_{ikj} \Big]}_{\eqqcolon \, K_{kij}}.
        \end{align*}</span>  The first term is the <strong>Levi-Civita</strong> connection, the unique torsion-free metric compatible one, symmetric in <span class="math inline">\(i, j\)</span>; the second is the <strong>contorsion</strong>, linear in the torsion. Its antisymmetric part reproduces the torsion, <span class="math inline">\(K_{kij} - K_{kji} = - \mathtt{T}_{kij}\)</span>, but its symmetric part does <em>not</em> vanish in general:  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \Gamma^k_{(ij)} = \mathring{\Gamma}^k_{ij} + \frac{1}{2} \, g^{km} \Big[ \mathtt{T}_{imj} + \mathtt{T}_{jmi} \Big].
        \end{align*}</span></p></li>
<li><p><strong>Statement B.</strong> For a fixed metric, the autoparallels of the metric compatible connection with torsion <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}\)</span> satisfy  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \ddot{\gamma}^k_\mathcal{U} + \mathring{\Gamma}^k_{ji} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}
            + g^{km} \, \mathtt{T}_{imj} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U} = 0,
        \end{align*}</span>  so torsion does affect them. The additional term vanishes for all velocities if and only if <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}_{imj} = - \mathtt{T}_{jmi}\)</span>, which, combined with the antisymmetry of torsion in its last two indices, means that <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}_{kij}\)</span> is <strong>totally antisymmetric</strong>. Only then are the autoparallels those of the Levi-Civita connection.</p></li>
</ul>
```

## `<span class="dg-secnum">B.22.3</span> Conclusion`{=html} {#subsection_Torsion_Resolution}

```{=html}
<p>The two statements describe different families of connections:</p>
<ol class="dg-enumerate dg-depth-1">
<li class="dg-labelled"><span class="dg-item-label">(A)</span> <p>fixing <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^k_{(ij)}\)</span> and varying <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}\)</span> leaves the autoparallels unchanged, but in general destroys metric compatibility;</p></li>
<li class="dg-labelled"><span class="dg-item-label">(B)</span> <p>fixing <span class="math inline">\(g\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\nabla g = 0\)</span> and varying <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}\)</span> preserves metric compatibility, but in general changes <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^k_{(ij)}\)</span>, hence the autoparallels.</p></li>
</ol>
<p>They agree precisely for totally antisymmetric torsion. Asking whether torsion affects autoparallels is therefore not meaningful until the structure from which the connection is built is specified.</p>
```

## `<span class="dg-secnum">B.22.4</span> Torsion Beyond Autoparallels`{=html} {#subsection_Torsion_Parallel_Transport}

```{=html}
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>Even in case (A), torsion is not invisible to the connection: it affects the parallel transport of vectors other than the velocity. Along a curve <span class="math inline">\(\gamma\)</span>, a vector field <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}_\gamma\)</span> with components <span class="math inline">\(x^k_\gamma\)</span> is parallel transported if  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \frac{d x^k_\gamma}{d\lambda} + \Gamma^k_{ji} \, x^j_\gamma \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} = 0,
        \end{align*}</span>  where <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma\)</span> is contracted with two <em>different</em> vectors, so its antisymmetric part contributes. Only for <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}_\gamma = v_\gamma\)</span>, which yields the autoparallel equation, does it drop out. Since the curvature measures the failure of parallel transport around closed curves, <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Riem}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Ric}\)</span> depend on the torsion as well: if <span class="math inline">\(\tilde{\nabla}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span> differ only by torsion, they have the same autoparallels but, in general, different curvatures.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Example.</strong> In a stratified chart of a Newtonian spacetime with all <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^i_{jk} = 0\)</span>, i.e. without gravity, add <span class="math inline">\(\tilde{\Gamma}^\alpha_{\beta\delta} \coloneqq \varepsilon_{\alpha\beta\delta}\)</span>, the totally antisymmetric symbol with <span class="math inline">\(\varepsilon_{123} = 1\)</span>. The new connection still satisfies <span class="math inline">\(\nabla dt = 0\)</span>, its torsion is <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}^\alpha_{\beta\delta} = - 2 \, \varepsilon_{\alpha\beta\delta}\)</span>, and its autoparallels are unchanged: free particles move along straight lines at constant velocity <span class="math inline">\(u^\alpha\)</span>. A spatial vector transported along such a worldline, however, obeys <span class="math inline">\(\frac{d x^\alpha_\gamma}{dt} = - \varepsilon_{\alpha\beta\delta} \, x^\beta_\gamma \, u^\delta\)</span>: it rotates about the direction of motion. Correspondingly, by the component expression of <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Riem}\)</span> (Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Covariant_Derivative">6</a>),  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \widetilde{\mathrm{Riem}}^\alpha_{\beta\delta\kappa} = \delta_{\alpha\kappa} \, \delta_{\beta\delta} - \delta_{\alpha\delta} \, \delta_{\beta\kappa},
            \qquad
            \widetilde{\mathrm{Ric}}_{\beta\kappa} = - 2 \, \delta_{\beta\kappa}:
        \end{align*}</span>  a spacetime with no gravity, in which every free particle moves exactly as in the torsion-free case, has non-vanishing curvature, and even violates the vacuum field equation <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Ric} = 0\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p>Torsion also enters two further results of Chapter <a class="dg-xref" href="../covariant-derivative/index.html" data-kind="chapter" data-label="chapter_Covariant_Derivative">6</a>. A chart with all <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^i_{jk} = 0\)</span> exists only if both <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Riem}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}\)</span> vanish, since torsion, being a tensor field, cannot be removed by any choice of chart. And the identification of the relative acceleration of neighbouring autoparallels with the curvature, as in the tidal acceleration of Section <a class="dg-xref" href="../newtonian/pseudo-forces.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Pseudo_Forces">9.4</a>, acquires torsion terms, so that with torsion it no longer equals <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Riem}\)</span>.</p></li>
</ul>
```

## `<span class="dg-secnum">B.22.5</span> The Newtonian Case`{=html} {#subsection_Torsion_Newtonian}

```{=html}
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>Uniform flow restricts torsion even before choosing the connection. The derivation <span class="math inline">\(\big( \nabla_{\partial x_i} dt \big)_k = - \Gamma^0_{ki}\)</span> of Section <a class="dg-xref" href="../newtonian/stratified-atlas.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Stratified_Atlas">9.3</a> does not use torsion-freeness, so <span class="math inline">\(\nabla dt = 0\)</span> gives <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^0_{ki} = 0\)</span> for all <span class="math inline">\(k, i\)</span>, and hence <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}^0_{jk} = 0\)</span>: the torsion of any connection compatible with absolute time is <strong>spatial</strong>.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Within Newton’s axioms, torsion is a gauge freedom.</strong> The axioms of Section <a class="dg-xref" href="../newtonian/newton-axioms.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Newton_Axioms">9.2</a> only involve worldlines, i.e. velocities transported along themselves. Free particles therefore determine <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^k_{(ij)}\)</span>, since knowing <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^k_{(ij)} \, \dot{\gamma}^i_\mathcal{U} \, \dot{\gamma}^j_\mathcal{U}\)</span> for all velocities fixes the symmetric part, but leave the torsion completely free, and no prediction depends on it. Requiring <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T} = 0\)</span> selects the unique connection determined by free particles. It is a convention, but a necessary one: only for this connection do <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Riem}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Ric}\)</span> depend on observable quantities alone, so that <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Riem} \neq 0\)</span> signals gravity, <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Ric} = 4 \pi G \rho \; dt\left\lceil \cdot \right\rfloor dt\left\lceil \cdot \right\rfloor\)</span> ties curvature to matter, and <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{Riem}^\alpha_{0\beta0}\)</span> is the tidal acceleration. With torsion, the curvature would also record the unobservable rotation of the example above.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Beyond Newton’s axioms, torsion is physical.</strong> If parallel transport of vectors other than the velocity is given physical meaning, torsion becomes observable, and its value is decided by experiment rather than by convention. Two instances:</p>
<ol class="dg-enumerate dg-depth-1">
<li><p><em>Gyroscopes.</em> Postulating that the axis of a torque-free gyroscope is parallel transported, the torsion of the example would make it precess about the direction of motion. Experience shows that a torque-free gyroscope keeps its orientation w.r.t. non-rotating axes, i.e. is parallel transported by the torsion-free connection.</p></li>
<li><p><em>Spatial metric.</em> If <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span> is required to be compatible with a spatial metric <span class="math inline">\(h\)</span> (Appendix <span class="dg-xref dg-xref-pending" data-label="section_Newtonian_Formulations">B.21</span>), Statement B applies to the spatial indices: in a Cartesian stratified chart, spatial torsion that is not totally antisymmetric in its three spatial indices changes <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma^\alpha_{(\beta\delta)}\)</span>, and hence the worldlines themselves.</p></li>
</ol>
<p>In both cases the torsion-free condition becomes a physical assumption, consistent with Newtonian experience. The definition of Newtonian spacetime thus fixes the gauge freedom left by the axioms in the one way compatible with these further observations.</p></li>
</ul>
<section class="dg-footnotes" role="doc-endnotes"><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-10" role="doc-footnote"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-10" aria-label="Back to the text">10</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>Write the compatibility condition three times, cyclically permuting <span class="math inline">\((i, j, k)\)</span>, and add the first two minus the third. Replacing every <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma_{mab}\)</span> by <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma_{mba} - \mathtt{T}_{mab}\)</span> where needed, all terms except <span class="math inline">\(2 \, \Gamma_{kij}\)</span> cancel or combine into torsion terms, which yields the expression given. Conversely, this expression satisfies the compatibility condition and has torsion <span class="math inline">\(\mathtt{T}\)</span>. <span class="math inline">\(\square\)</span></p></div></div></section>
```
